distribution: Worldwide; particularly problematic in greenhouse and field-grown tomatoes

seedlings: Young plants may show poor growth or temporary branch wilting
mature_plants_systemic: Curling, yellowing, wilting, and browning (firing) of oldest leaflets
Stunted growth and general plant wilting
Yellow to reddish-brown pith with mealy appearance
Stem streaks, branch breakage, and potential plant death
mature_plants_secondary: Dark brown to almost black lesions on leaf margins
Fruit: yellow to brown raised spots with persistent white halo ('bird's eye' spots), ~3 mm in diameter
Vascular tissue under calyx may be discolored, affecting seeds

disease_cycle.overwintering: Up to 3 years on plant residue; in weeds; on greenhouse materials (benches, stakes, flats)
spread: Overhead irrigation splash from infected plants
Direct contact with infected plants or equipment
disease_cycle.entry: Bacteria enter seedlings through small wounds in cotyledons and move systemically through xylem

prevention: Strict monitoring of seed fields; discard contaminated lots
Soak seed in 130°F water for 25 minutes
greenhouse_measures: Disinfect benches, flats, and irrigation hoses
field_measures: Avoid working when foliage is wet
Incorporate all plant tissue at season's end
Rotate fields out of tomato for at least one year
chemical_control: Repeated copper applications may reduce disease spread but are not fully reliable
Surface disinfectants: bleach (0.5–1% calcium or sodium hypochlorite), Physan, etc.

notes: Economic losses in direct-seeded fields are usually uncommon
Seed contamination with very few bacteria can lead to significant greenhouse infection
Systemic infections cannot be cured with bactericides; focus is on prevention and sanitation
